name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_1 - Meaning of uniform translatory motion

questiontext.text: 5.1 A ball is travelling with uniform translatory motion. This means that

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Translatory motion is the motion of a body in which all its constituent particles move through the same displacement in the same interval of time without any rotation about an axis. Uniform motion means that the velocity remains constant in both magnitude and direction.

Step 2: Evaluation
For a ball undergoing uniform translatory motion, it cannot be at rest unless its constant velocity is zero, nor can it move along a circular path (where direction continuously changes) or spin about its centre (which introduces rotational motion where different parts have different velocities).

Step 3: Application
Therefore, every part of the ball must have the exact same velocity vector—both in magnitude and in direction—and this velocity must remain constant over time.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Uniform translatory motion means that all parts of the ball have the same velocity (magnitude and direction) and the velocity is constant.

answer.text: it is at rest.
the path can be a straight line or circular and the ball travels with uniform speed.
all parts of the ball have the same velocity (magnitude and direction) and the velocity is constant.
the centre of the ball moves with constant velocity and the ball spins about its centre uniformly.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_2 - Force and torque for uniform velocity

questiontext.text: 5.2 A metre scale is moving with uniform velocity. This implies

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's second law of motion, the net external force \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}}\) acting on a body of mass \(m\) is proportional to its linear acceleration \(\mathbf{a}\): \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\mathbf{a}\). Similarly, for rotational motion about the centre of mass, the net external torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}}\) is given by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} = I\boldsymbol{\alpha}\), where \(I\) is the moment of inertia and \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) is the angular acceleration.

Step 2: Evaluation
Since the metre scale is moving with uniform velocity, every particle of the scale has constant linear velocity. Thus, its linear acceleration is zero (\(\mathbf{a} = 0\)) and it has no angular acceleration (\(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = 0\)).

Step 3: Application
Substituting \(\mathbf{a} = 0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = 0\) into the equations of motion gives \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = 0\) and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} = 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The net force acting on the scale is zero and the net torque acting about the centre of mass of the scale is also zero.

answer.text: the force acting on the scale is zero, but a torque about the centre of mass can act on the scale.
the force acting on the scale is zero and the torque acting about centre of mass of the scale is also zero.
the total force acting on it need not be zero but the torque on it is zero.
neither the force nor the torque need to be zero.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_3 - Change in momentum of cricket ball

questiontext.text: 5.3 A cricket ball of mass \(150\text{ g}\) has an initial velocity \(\mathbf{u} = (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and a final velocity \(\mathbf{v} = -(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) after being hit. The change in momentum (final momentum-initial momentum) is (in \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the cricket ball, \(m = 150\text{ g} = 0.15\text{ kg}\).
Initial velocity, \(\mathbf{u} = (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Final velocity, \(\mathbf{v} = -(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Unit vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) represent mutually perpendicular orthogonal axes in the plane of motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Linear momentum is \(\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}\). The change in momentum is \(\Delta \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_f - \mathbf{p}_i = m(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Delta \mathbf{p} = 0.15\text{ kg} \times \left[-(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}}) - (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\right]\,\text{m s}^{-1}\]
\[\Delta \mathbf{p} = 0.15 \times (-6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 8\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\[\Delta \mathbf{p} = -(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{u}\), the change in momentum is \(-2m\mathbf{u}\), which matches \(-2(0.15)(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). The units are \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: \(-(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_4 - Magnitude of momentum transferred during hit

questiontext.text: 5.4 In the previous problem (5.3), the magnitude of the momentum transferred during the hit is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the previous problem, the ball has mass \(m = 150\text{ g} = 0.15\text{ kg}\), initial velocity \(\mathbf{u} = (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and final velocity \(\mathbf{v} = -(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The change in momentum is \(\Delta \mathbf{p} = -(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The momentum transferred has magnitude equal to the Euclidean norm of the vector \(\Delta \mathbf{p}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a vector \(\Delta \mathbf{p} = \Delta p_x \hat{\mathbf{i}} + \Delta p_y \hat{\mathbf{j}}\), its magnitude is \(|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{(\Delta p_x)^2 + (\Delta p_y)^2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{(-0.9)^2 + (-1.2)^2}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\[|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{0.81 + 1.44}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1} = \sqrt{2.25}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1} = 1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Alternatively, the speed is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and since velocity reverses completely, \(|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = 2mv = 2 \times 0.15 \times 5 = 1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: \(1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_5 - Conservation of momentum from Newton's laws

questiontext.text: 5.5 Conservation of momentum in a collision between particles can be understood from

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Consider an isolated system of two colliding particles. By Newton's third law of motion, during the collision, the force \(\mathbf{F}_{12}\) exerted by the second particle on the first is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force \(\mathbf{F}_{21}\) exerted by the first particle on the second: \(\mathbf{F}_{12} = -\mathbf{F}_{21}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
By Newton's second law of motion, the force on each particle equals the rate of change of its linear momentum: \(\mathbf{F}_{12} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}_1}{dt}\) and \(\mathbf{F}_{21} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}_2}{dt}\).

Step 3: Application
Combining both laws yields \(\frac{d\mathbf{p}_1}{dt} + \frac{d\mathbf{p}_2}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf{p}_1 + \mathbf{p}_2) = 0\), which implies that the total linear momentum \(\mathbf{p}_1 + \mathbf{p}_2\) remains constant during the collision.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Conservation of momentum in a collision between particles can be understood from both Newton's second and third law.

answer.text: conservation of energy.
Newton's first law only.
Newton's second law only.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_6 - Force on hockey player turning westward

questiontext.text: 5.6 A hockey player is moving northward and suddenly turns westward with the same speed to avoid an opponent. The force that acts on the player is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Newton's second law, the net external force \(\mathbf{F}\) acting on a body is in the direction of the change in momentum \(\Delta \mathbf{p} = m(\mathbf{v}_f - \mathbf{v}_i)\). Internal muscular forces cannot change the momentum of the player's centre of mass; an external horizontal force must be provided by friction between the player's shoes/skates and the ground.

Step 2: Evaluation
Let the northward direction be \(+\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and the eastward direction be \(+\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (so westward is \(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) and southward is \(-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\)).
Initial velocity: \(\mathbf{v}_i = v\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).
Final velocity: \(\mathbf{v}_f = -v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\).

Step 3: Application
The change in velocity is \(\Delta \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_f - \mathbf{v}_i = -v\hat{\mathbf{i}} - v\hat{\mathbf{j}}\). Since both the westward (\(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}\)) and southward (\(-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\)) components are equal and negative, \(\Delta \mathbf{v}\) (and hence \(\Delta \mathbf{p}\) and the external force \(\mathbf{F}\)) is directed along the south-west direction. This external force is the frictional force exerted by the surface.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The force that acts on the player is the frictional force along south-west.

answer.text: frictional force along westward.
muscle force along southward.
frictional force along south-west.
muscle force along south-west.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_7 - Force acting on body from position-time law

questiontext.text: 5.7 A body of mass \(2\text{ kg}\) travels according to the law \(x(t) = pt + qt^2 + rt^3\) where \(p = 3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(q = 4\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and \(r = 5\,\text{m s}^{-3}\). The force acting on the body at \(t = 2\text{ seconds}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the body, \(m = 2\text{ kg}\).
Position as a function of time: \(x(t) = pt + qt^2 + rt^3\), with \(p = 3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(q = 4\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), \(r = 5\,\text{m s}^{-3}\).
Time instant: \(t = 2\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is one-dimensional along the \(x\)-axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity \(v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}\), acceleration \(a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}\), and force \(F(t) = m a(t)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating \(x(t)\) with respect to \(t\):
\[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = p + 2qt + 3rt^2\]
Differentiating \(v(t)\) with respect to \(t\):
\[a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 2q + 6rt\]
At \(t = 2\text{ s}\):
\[a(2) = 2(4\,\text{m s}^{-2}) + 6(5\,\text{m s}^{-3})(2\text{ s}) = 8 + 60 = 68\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
Force at \(t = 2\text{ s}\):
\[F = m a(2) = 2\text{ kg} \times 68\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 136\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Every term in \(a(t)\) has units of \(\text{m s}^{-2}\), and \(F = ma\) has units of \(\text{kg m s}^{-2} = \text{N}\).
Final Answer: \(136\text{ N}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_8 - Time when velocity is along y-axis

questiontext.text: 5.8 A body with mass \(5\text{ kg}\) is acted upon by a force \(\mathbf{F} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\text{ N}\). If its initial velocity at \(t = 0\) is \(\mathbf{v} = (6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 12\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the time at which it will just have a velocity along the \(y\)-axis is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass, \(m = 5\text{ kg}\).
Constant force, \(\mathbf{F} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\text{ N}\).
Initial velocity at \(t = 0\), \(\mathbf{u} = (6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 12\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion takes place in the \(xy\)-plane under a constant force, so acceleration is constant. For the velocity to be purely along the \(y\)-axis, its \(x\)-component must be zero (\(v_x = 0\)) while its \(y\)-component is non-zero (\(v_y \neq 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Acceleration \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{F}}{m}\), and velocity at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The \(x\)-component of acceleration is:
\[a_x = \frac{F_x}{m} = \frac{-3\text{ N}}{5\text{ kg}} = -0.6\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
Setting the \(x\)-component of velocity to zero:
\[v_x(t) = u_x + a_x t = 6 - 0.6t = 0\]
\[0.6t = 6 \implies t = \frac{6}{0.6} = 10\text{ s}\]
Checking the \(y\)-component at \(t = 10\text{ s}\):
\[a_y = \frac{F_y}{m} = \frac{4}{5} = 0.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
\[v_y(10) = -12 + 0.8(10) = -12 + 8 = -4\,\text{m s}^{-1} \neq 0\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(t = 10\text{ s}\), \(\mathbf{v} = -4\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), which is purely along the \(y\)-axis.
Final Answer: \(10\text{ s}\).

answer.text: never

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_9 - External force accelerating a car eastward

questiontext.text: 5.9 A car of mass \(m\) starts from rest and acquires a velocity along east \(\mathbf{v} = v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (\(v > 0\)) in two seconds. Assuming the car moves with uniform acceleration, the force exerted on the car is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the car = \(m\), initial velocity \(\mathbf{u} = 0\), final velocity \(\mathbf{v} = v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (along east, with \(v > 0\)), and time taken \(t = 2\text{ s}\). The acceleration is uniform.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) points eastward. The car is treated as a system of mass \(m\), so only external forces can accelerate its centre of mass.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Uniform acceleration: \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}}{t}\).
Newton's second law: \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = m\mathbf{a}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The acceleration of the car is:
\[\mathbf{a} = \frac{v\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 0}{2} = \frac{v}{2}\hat{\mathbf{i}}\]
The net external force on the car is:
\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} = \frac{mv}{2}\hat{\mathbf{i}} (eastward).
Because the car's engine is an internal part of the car, it cannot exert a net external force on the car as a whole. Instead, the engine rotates the tyres, which push the road backward, and by Newton's third law, the road exerts a forward static frictional force on the tyres.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The force has magnitude \(\frac{mv}{2}\) directed eastward and is due to the friction on the tyres exerted by the road.
Final Answer: \(\frac{mv}{2}\) eastward and is due to the friction on the tyres exerted by the road.

answer.text: \(\frac{mv}{2}\) eastward and is exerted by the car engine.
\(\frac{mv}{2}\) eastward and is due to the friction on the tyres exerted by the road.
more than \(\frac{mv}{2}\) eastward exerted due to the engine and overcomes the friction of the road.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_10 - Force and impulse for sinusoidal motion

questiontext.text: 5.10 The motion of a particle of mass \(m\) is given by \(x = 0\) for \(t < 0\text{ s}\), \(x(t) = A \sin 4\pi t\) for \(0 < t < (1/4)\text{ s}\) (\(A > 0\)), and \(x = 0\) for \(t > (1/4)\text{ s}\). Which of the following statements is true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of particle = \(m\).
Position \(x(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\text{ s}\) and \(t > \frac{1}{4}\text{ s}\).
Position \(x(t) = A\sin(4\pi t)\) for \(0 < t < \frac{1}{4}\text{ s}\), with \(A > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is one-dimensional along the \(x\)-axis. Discontinuities in velocity correspond to instantaneous impulses.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity \(v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}\), acceleration \(a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}\), force \(F(t) = m a(t)\), and impulse \(J = \Delta p = m(v_f - v_i)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(0 < t < \frac{1}{4}\text{ s}\):
\[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 4\pi A \cos(4\pi t)\]
\[a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -16\pi^2 A \sin(4\pi t)\]
\[F(t) = m a(t) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin(4\pi t)\]
Since \(F(t)\) varies sinusoidally with time \(t\), the particle is not acted upon by a constant force.
At \(t = \frac{1}{8}\text{ s}\):
\[F\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin\left(4\pi \times \frac{1}{8}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m\]
At \(t = 0\text{ s}\), velocity jumps from \(0\) (for \(t < 0\)) to \(v(0^+) = 4\pi A \cos(0) = 4\pi A\), so an impulse of magnitude \(4\pi A m\) acts on the particle. Similarly, at \(t = \frac{1}{4}\text{ s}\), velocity jumps from \(v((1/4)^-) = 4\pi A \cos(\pi) = -4\pi A\) to \(0\) (for \(t > \frac{1}{4}\)), giving an impulse of magnitude \(4\pi A m\) (printed as \(4\pi^2 A m\) in the source text).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The force at \(t = (1/8)\text{ s}\) is \(-16\pi^2 A m\), impulses act at \(t = 0\text{ s}\) and \(t = (1/4)\text{ s}\), and the force acting during \(0 < t < (1/4)\text{ s}\) is not constant.

answer.text: The force at \(t = (1/8)\text{ s}\) on the particle is \(-16\pi^2 A\,m\).
The particle is acted upon by an impulse of magnitude \(4\pi^2 A\,m\) at \(t = 0\text{ s}\) and \(t = (1/4)\text{ s}\).
The particle is not acted upon by any force.
The particle is not acted upon by a constant force.
There is no impulse acting on the particle.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_11 - Friction between two stacked blocks

questiontext.text: 5.11 In Fig. 5.1, the co-efficient of friction between the floor and the body B is \(0.1\). The co-efficient of friction between the bodies B and A is \(0.2\). A force \(\mathbf{F}\) is applied as shown on B. The mass of A is \(m/2\) and of B is \(m\). Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of block A, \(m_A = \frac{m}{2}\); mass of block B, \(m_B = m\).
Coefficient of friction between B and the floor, \(\mu_1 = 0.1\).
Coefficient of friction between A and B, \(\mu_2 = 0.2\).
A horizontal force \(\mathbf{F}\) is applied to the lower block B.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The static and kinetic coefficients of friction are assumed equal. Block A accelerates solely due to the frictional force exerted on it by block B.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Limiting friction \(f_{\max} = \mu N\).
Newton's second law: \(F_{\text{net}} = m_{\text{total}} a\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Limiting friction between B and the floor:
\[f_{1,\max} = \mu_1 (m_A + m_B) g = 0.1 \times \left(\frac{m}{2} + m\right) g = 0.1 \times 1.5 mg = 0.15 mg\]
Thus, for \(F \le 0.15 mg\) (for instance, \(F = 0.1 mg\)), the system remains at rest.
2. Limiting friction between A and B:
\[f_{2,\max} = \mu_2 m_A g = 0.2 \times \frac{m}{2} g = 0.1 mg\]
Maximum acceleration of A before slipping:
\[a_{\max} = \frac{f_{2,\max}}{m_A} = \mu_2 g = 0.2 g\]
3. Maximum applied force \(F_{\max}\) for which both bodies move together:
\[F_{\max} - f_{1,\max} = (m_A + m_B) a_{\max}\]
\[F_{\max} = 0.15 mg + 1.5 m (0.2 g) = 0.15 mg + 0.30 mg = 0.45 mg\]
Therefore:
- For \(F = 0.25 mg\): since \(0.15 mg < 0.25 mg \le 0.45 mg\), both bodies move together.
- For \(F = 0.5 mg\): since \(0.5 mg > 0.45 mg\), body A slips with respect to B.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The true statements are: the bodies move together if \(F = 0.25 mg\); body A slips with respect to B if \(F = 0.5 mg\); the bodies remain at rest if \(F = 0.1 mg\); and the maximum value of \(F\) for moving together is \(0.45 mg\).

answer.text: The bodies will move together if \(F = 0.25\,mg\).
The body A will slip with respect to B if \(F = 0.5\,mg\).
The bodies will move together if \(F = 0.5\,mg\).
The bodies will be at rest if \(F = 0.1\,mg\).
The maximum value of \(F\) for which the two bodies will move together is \(0.45\,mg\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_12 - Motion of connected masses on an incline

questiontext.text: 5.12 Mass \(m_1\) moves on a slope making an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal and is attached to mass \(m_2\) by a string passing over a frictionless pulley as shown in Fig. 5.2. The co-efficient of friction between \(m_1\) and the sloping surface is \(\mu\). Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass \(m_1\) rests on a rough inclined plane of angle \(\theta\) with coefficient of friction \(\mu\). It is connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley to a vertically hanging mass \(m_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The string is light and inextensible, and the pulley is frictionless. Friction always opposes the impending or actual relative motion of \(m_1\) along the incline.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Normal reaction on \(m_1\): \(N = m_1 g \cos\theta\).
Maximum frictional force: \(f_{\max} = \mu N = \mu m_1 g \cos\theta\).
Component of weight of \(m_1\) down the incline: \(m_1 g \sin\theta\).
Downward gravitational pull on \(m_2\): \(m_2 g\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Condition for \(m_1\) to move up the plane: The pulling force \(m_2 g\) must overcome both the down-slope weight component and the downward-acting friction:
\[m_2 g > m_1 g \sin\theta + \mu m_1 g \cos\theta\]
Dividing by \(g\):
\[m_2 > m_1 (\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta)\]
2. Condition for \(m_1\) to move down the plane: The down-slope weight component must overcome both \(m_2 g\) and the upward-acting friction:
\[m_1 g \sin\theta > m_2 g + \mu m_1 g \cos\theta\]
Rearranging:
\[m_2 < m_1 (\sin\theta - \mu \cos\theta)\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The body \(m_1\) moves up the plane if \(m_2 > m_1(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)\) and moves down the plane if \(m_2 < m_1(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)\).

answer.text: If \(m_2 > m_1 \sin\theta\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 > m_1 (\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta)\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta)\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin\theta - \mu \cos\theta)\), the body will move down the plane.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_13 - Two blocks on double inclined plane

questiontext.text: 5.13 In Fig. 5.3, a body A of mass \(m\) slides on plane inclined at angle \(\theta_1\) to the horizontal and \(\mu_1\) is the coefficient of friction between A and the plane. A is connected by a light string passing over a frictionless pulley to another body B, also of mass \(m\), sliding on a frictionless plane inclined at angle \(\theta_2\) to the horizontal. Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Body A (mass \(m\)) is on a rough incline of angle \(\theta_1\) with coefficient of friction \(\mu_1\) (denoted \(\mu\) in the condition). Body B (mass \(m\)) is on a frictionless incline of angle \(\theta_2\). They are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) lie between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). When A tends to move up its incline, friction on A acts down the incline.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Down-slope gravitational component on A: \(mg\sin\theta_1\).
Limiting friction on A: \(f_{\max} = \mu mg\cos\theta_1\).
Down-slope gravitational component on B: \(mg\sin\theta_2\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For A to just start moving up the plane, the pull from B must balance the down-slope component of A's weight plus the limiting friction on A:
\[mg\sin\theta_2 = mg\sin\theta_1 + \mu mg\cos\theta_1\]
Solving for \(\mu\):
\[\mu = \frac{\sin\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1}{\cos\theta_1}\]
Furthermore, for A to move up the plane, we require \(\sin\theta_2 > \sin\theta_1 + \mu\cos\theta_1\). Since \(\mu \ge 0\) and \(\cos\theta_1 > 0\), this requires \(\sin\theta_2 > \sin\theta_1\), which means \(\theta_2 > \theta_1\) is always necessary. Note that A can move up if \(\theta_2\) is sufficiently larger than \(\theta_1\), and B accelerates rather than always sliding at constant speed.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A will just start moving up the plane when \(\mu = \frac{\sin\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1}{\cos\theta_1}\), and for A to move up the plane, \(\theta_2\) must always be greater than \(\theta_1\).

answer.text: A will never move up the plane.
A will just start moving up the plane when \(\mu = \frac{\sin\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1}{\cos\theta_1}\).
For A to move up the plane, \(\theta_2\) must always be greater than \(\theta_1\).
B will always slide down with constant speed.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_14 - Impulse and force in billiard ball collision

questiontext.text: 5.14 Two billiard balls A and B, each of mass \(50\text{ g}\) and moving in opposite directions with speed of \(5\text{ m s}^{-1}\) each, collide and rebound with the same speed. If the collision lasts for \(10^{-3}\text{ s}\), which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of each ball, \(m = 50\text{ g} = 0.05\text{ kg}\).
Initial speed, \(u = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}\); rebound speed, \(v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}\) (in opposite direction).
Duration of collision, \(\Delta t = 10^{-3}\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Take the initial velocity of ball A as \(+5\text{ m s}^{-1}\), so its final velocity is \(-5\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Impulse \(J = |\Delta p| = m|v - u|\).
Average force \(F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{J}{\Delta t}\).
By Newton's third law, \(\mathbf{F}_{AB} = -\mathbf{F}_{BA}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Magnitude of impulse imparted to each ball:
\[J = 0.05\text{ kg} \times |-5 - 5|\,\text{m s}^{-1} = 0.05 \times 10 = 0.5\text{ N s} = 0.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
Magnitude of average force on each ball:
\[F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{0.5\text{ N s}}{10^{-3}\text{ s}} = 500\text{ N}\]
By Newton's third law, the forces exerted on the two balls during the collision are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Since the collision duration \(\Delta t\) is the same for both balls, the impulses imparted to each ball are also equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.5\text{ N s}\) (and the average force is \(500\text{ N}\)), and the impulse and the force on each ball are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

answer.text: The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.25\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and the force on each ball is \(250\text{ N}\).
The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.25\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and the force exerted on each ball is \(25 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}\).
The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.5\text{ Ns}\).
The impulse and the force on each ball are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWSOFMOTION_Q5_15 - Resultant acceleration from perpendicular forces

questiontext.text: 5.15 A body of mass \(10\text{ kg}\) is acted upon by two perpendicular forces, \(6\text{ N}\) and \(8\text{ N}\). The resultant acceleration of the body is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the body, \(m = 10\text{ kg}\).
Two perpendicular forces: \(F_1 = 6\text{ N}\) and \(F_2 = 8\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The \(6\text{ N}\) force and \(8\text{ N}\) force are at \(90^\circ\) to each other.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resultant of two perpendicular forces: \(F = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2}\).
Magnitude of acceleration: \(a = \frac{F}{m}\).
Direction angle \(\theta\) with respect to \(F_1\): \(\tan\theta = \frac{F_2}{F_1}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Magnitude of the resultant force:
\[F = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ N}\]
Magnitude of the resultant acceleration:
\[a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{10\text{ N}}{10\text{ kg}} = 1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
Angle \(\theta_1\) with respect to the \(6\text{ N}\) force:
\[\tan\theta_1 = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\]
Angle \(\theta_2\) with respect to the \(8\text{ N}\) force:
\[\tan\theta_2 = \frac{6}{8} = \frac{3}{4} \implies \theta_2 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Note that \(\tan^{-1}(4/3) + \tan^{-1}(3/4) = 90^\circ\), confirming consistency. Thus, the resultant acceleration is \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) w.r.t. the \(6\text{ N}\) force, or equivalently at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) w.r.t. the \(8\text{ N}\) force.

answer.text: \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) w.r.t. \(6\text{ N}\) force.
\(0.2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) w.r.t. \(6\text{ N}\) force.
\(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) w.r.t. \(8\text{ N}\) force.
\(0.2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) w.r.t. \(8\text{ N}\) force.
